claims.text: A targeted post-solidification thermomechanical treatment can induce coherent precipitates in a eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The induced precipitates will be nanoscale, uniformly distributed, and located along and within the eutectic lamellar colonies.
The precipitate-forming treatment will simultaneously improve room-temperature tensile strength and ductility.
The initial eutectic alloy has wide, microcrack-prone internal boundaries within dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Intermediate cold deformation followed by aging is an effective route for producing coherent precipitation structures.
Aging will precipitate a secondary coherent phase analogous to γ″ particles at the lamellar interfaces.
Controlled cooling and aging will maintain precipitate coherency.
The structural mediator is a population of uniformly distributed nanoscale coherent precipitates along lamellar boundaries.
Coherent precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and thereby increase strength.
Precipitates at internal boundaries blunt stress concentrations and reduce crack initiation.
Reduced crack initiation will permit higher tensile ductility than in the coarse, unmodified lamellar structure.
The treated alloy will have higher ultimate tensile strength at room temperature than the unmodified baseline.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile elongation before fracture than the unmodified baseline.
The conventionally processed baseline has coarse lamellar colonies in which internal-boundary microcracking limits tensile ductility.
The simultaneous strength-and-ductility benefit requires the precipitates to remain nanoscale and coherent.
Precipitate coarsening or loss of coherency may reverse the benefit and cause embrittlement.
The magnitudes of the strength and ductility changes will depend on precipitate size, spacing, and distribution and on processing temperature and deformation level.

contradictions.description: The intervention is defined as a two-step route containing intermediate cold deformation followed by aging, but the treated experimental group is described only as receiving an additional aging step, so the proposed test does not clearly implement the stated intervention.

The benefit is explicitly conditioned on forming and retaining nanoscale coherent precipitates, yet failure to form those precipitates is labeled as falsification. Such a result would show failure to instantiate the intervention or satisfy its boundary conditions, rather than decisively refuting the proposed precipitate-mediated effect.
